title: Continuing professional development
blurb: Explain why CPD must cover knowledge, skills and behaviours, and how you identify and close your own competence gaps.
question: A project manager's sponsor says her board updates are too technical, and she has never used the new risk tool her organisation has adopted. Who is responsible for identifying and closing these gaps, and how should she approach it through continuing professional development?

teach.body: Continuing professional development (CPD) is the ongoing, planned process of maintaining and developing your knowledge, skills and behaviours throughout your career, so your competence stays current as the profession changes. In plain English: keep getting better deliberately, not by accident, and keep a record of it. It is continuous: not a course you take once at the start of a career.

rows.label: Means
values: What you can do in practice

teach.caption: Competence is the combination of knowledge, skills and behaviours. Neglect any one and performance suffers.

teach.body: The INDIVIDUAL is responsible for identifying and addressing their own competence gaps. Employers, sponsors and mentors can support with feedback, time and funding, but they cannot do it for you. Why it matters: methods, technology and regulations keep changing; up-to-date professionals deliver better projects and earn credibility with stakeholders; and CPD supports career progression, for example towards Chartered Project Professional (ChPP) status.

teach.caption: Self-assess against the APM Competence Framework, gather feedback, plan goals, learn, reflect on what changed in practice, and record it. Then go round again.

children.label: New demands
children.sub: a new role, method or tool

Examples
Good for
teach.caption: Most activities develop more than one element. The best CPD plan mixes several types.

teach.text: Three traps. 1) CPD is not only knowledge: it must cover knowledge, skills AND behaviours. 2) It is not the employer's or HR's job to find your gaps: the INDIVIDUAL owns them. 3) It is continuous and planned, not a one-off or something you do only when an appraisal is due.

teach.body: Amira self-assesses against the APM Competence Framework and asks her sponsor and team for feedback. She finds three gaps: board updates too technical (behaviour), the new risk tool (skill) and new building safety requirements (knowledge). Her plan: coaching on communicating with senior stakeholders, vendor training on the tool and a course on the regulations. After the next board meeting she reflects on what worked, and logs it all in her CPD record.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define CPD as ongoing, planned development of knowledge, skills AND behaviours.
State that the individual is responsible for identifying and closing their own gaps.
Describe how: self-assess (APM Competence Framework), seek feedback, plan, learn, reflect, record.
Give a varied example of activities (course, coaching, shadowing, reading).
Explain the benefit: current competence, better project performance, credibility, progression (e.g. ChPP).
CPD keeps knowledge, skills and behaviours current throughout a career.
The individual owns their competence gaps; others support.
Identify gaps by self-assessment against the APM Competence Framework, feedback and reviews.
Typical cycle: self-assess, seek feedback, plan, learn, reflect, record.
CPD supports better performance and progression, e.g. towards ChPP.

summary: You can now explain what CPD is, why it must cover knowledge, skills and behaviours, and why the individual owns their competence gaps. You can also describe how to identify gaps and work through a CPD cycle of planning, learning, reflecting and recording.

A.q: Continuing professional development should cover which of the following?
options: Technical knowledge only
Knowledge, skills and behaviours
Formal qualifications only
Skills for the current project only
A.why: CPD should develop all three elements of competence: knowledge, skills and behaviours.

whyNot.0: Knowledge alone isn't enough; how you apply it (skills) and how you act (behaviours) matter too.
whyNot.2: Qualifications are one CPD activity among many, not the whole of it.
whyNot.3: CPD looks across your career, not just the needs of today's project.

A.q: Who is primarily responsible for identifying a project professional's competence gaps?
options: Their line manager
The project sponsor
The professional themselves
The organisation's HR team
A.why: The individual is responsible for identifying and addressing their own competence gaps, with others supporting.

whyNot.0: A line manager can give feedback and support but doesn't own the individual's development.
whyNot.1: The sponsor may give useful feedback, but the gaps belong to the individual.
whyNot.3: HR may provide frameworks and funding, but it isn't responsible for spotting each person's gaps.

A.q: Which is the best description of CPD?
options: A course taken once at the start of a career
Training the employer must provide every year
An ongoing, planned process across a career
A test passed once to keep a job role secure
A.why: CPD is continuous and planned, running throughout a professional's career.

whyNot.0: CPD is continuing by definition, not a one-off at the start.
whyNot.1: Employers may support CPD, but it is not simply training they must provide.
whyNot.3: CPD is about ongoing development, not passing a single test.

B.q: Which activity is the best way to identify gaps in your behaviours?
options: Ask sponsor, team and stakeholders for feedback
Read the latest edition of a relevant standard
Count the training hours completed this year
Compare your salary with other managers
B.why: Behaviours are seen by others. Feedback from those you work with reveals how you come across, which self-review alone can miss.

whyNot.1: Reading a standard builds knowledge; it won't show how you behave with others.
whyNot.2: Hours completed measure input, not where your gaps are.
whyNot.3: Salary comparisons say nothing about your competence gaps.

B.q: A project manager learns to use new scheduling software. Which element of competence is this mainly developing?
options: Knowledge
Behaviours
Qualifications
Skills
B.why: Being able to use a tool in practice is a skill: what you can do.

whyNot.0: Knowledge is what you know and understand; operating software is a practical skill.
whyNot.1: Behaviours are how you act with others, such as listening or leading.
whyNot.2: Qualifications are a way of recognising competence, not one of its three elements.

B.q: After a course on negotiation, which step best completes the CPD cycle?
options: File the certificate and book the next one
Reflect on how practice changed and record it
Ask the employer to update the job description
Wait for the annual appraisal to discuss it
B.why: Reflection checks whether the learning has changed your practice, and recording it builds evidence for your development.

whyNot.0: Moving straight on skips reflection, so you can't tell whether the gap has closed.
whyNot.2: The job description isn't the issue; the point is your own development.
whyNot.3: CPD is continuous; waiting for an appraisal delays reflection and the next step.

C.q: A project manager receives feedback that she often interrupts team members in meetings. What is the most professional response?
options: Explain that it is just her personal style
Ask her manager to book a technical course
Wait to see if others raise the same point
Reflect, set a goal and seek some coaching
C.why: This is a behavioural gap she owns. Reflecting, setting a development goal and getting coaching is CPD in action.

whyNot.0: Dismissing feedback ignores a real competence gap in behaviour.
whyNot.1: A technical course targets knowledge or skills, not this behavioural gap, and she should own the plan.
whyNot.2: Waiting passes responsibility back to others and delays improvement.

C.q: In an iterative project, which regular event gives team members the most frequent chance to reflect on their own development needs?
options: The retrospective each iteration
The gate review each phase
The post-project review
The annual appraisal
C.why: Retrospectives at the end of every iteration give frequent feedback, so people can try a new behaviour and check its effect quickly.

whyNot.1: Gate reviews belong to linear life cycles and happen far less often.
whyNot.2: A post-project review happens once, at the end.
whyNot.3: An annual appraisal is useful but much less frequent.

C.q: Which is NOT a reason CPD matters for project professionals?
options: Methods and regulations keep changing
It supports progression, e.g. to ChPP
It hands competence gaps to the employer
It improves performance on projects
C.why: CPD does the opposite: the individual takes responsibility for their own competence gaps.

whyNot.0: A changing profession is a key reason to keep developing.
whyNot.1: CPD supports progression, for example towards Chartered Project Professional status.
whyNot.3: Current competence leads to better project performance.

reteach.title: Training for your next 10k run
reteach.question: Imagine you run 10k races. Nobody else can get you fitter, and last year's training won't win this year's race. How is that like CPD?

blocks.body: You time a test run (self-assess), ask a coach where you lose time (feedback), plan sessions for your weak spots (plan), train (learn), look at your next race time (reflect) and log it in your running app (record). A coach helps, but only you can do the running. Stop training and your fitness fades: competence works the same way.

blocks.text: Training only your legs won't do: you need stamina, technique and race tactics. CPD likewise needs knowledge, skills and behaviours.

explain.body: CPD is ongoing, planned development throughout your career. It matters because methods, technology and regulation change; current professionals deliver better projects, earn credibility and progress (for example towards ChPP).

test.q: A project manager qualified ten years ago and has done no development since, saying 'I already passed my exams'. What is the main risk?
options: Her competence may no longer be current
Her qualification has been withdrawn
She must now repeat the original exam
Her employer must take over her learning
test.why: Without CPD, knowledge, skills and behaviours fall behind changes in methods, technology and regulation.

whyNot.1: Not doing CPD doesn't by itself withdraw a past qualification; the issue is current competence.
whyNot.2: There is no general rule requiring her to retake an exam; the risk is out-of-date competence.
whyNot.3: Responsibility for development stays with the individual.

explain.body: Knowledge is what you know, skills are what you can do, behaviours are how you act. A project manager may know the theory of stakeholder engagement (knowledge), run a workshop (skill), and still alienate people by not listening (behaviour).

test.q: A project manager understands risk theory well, but team members say she dismisses their concerns. Which element of competence most needs development?
options: Knowledge
Skills
Behaviours
Qualifications
test.why: Dismissing people's concerns is about how she acts with others: a behavioural gap.

whyNot.0: Her knowledge of risk theory is already strong.
whyNot.1: The issue isn't a practical technique but how she responds to people.
whyNot.3: Qualifications recognise competence; they aren't one of its three elements.

explain.body: The individual identifies and addresses their own competence gaps. Sources include self-assessment against the APM Competence Framework, feedback from others, lessons learned and the demands of a new role or tool.

test.q: Which tool helps a project professional self-assess their competence against a recognised set of standards?
options: The risk register
The APM Competence Framework
The project management plan
The benefits profile
test.why: The APM Competence Framework describes the competences expected of project professionals, so it is the basis for self-assessment.

whyNot.0: The risk register records project risks, not personal competence.
whyNot.2: The PMP sets out how the project will be managed.
whyNot.3: A benefits profile describes a benefit and how it will be measured.

explain.body: Turn gaps into goals in a development plan, choose a mix of activities, then reflect on what actually changed in practice and record it. The record shows progress and feeds the next cycle.

test.q: Why is recording CPD activity and reflections worthwhile?
options: It replaces the need to reflect
It is only needed for disputes
It means no feedback is needed
It evidences progress for next time
test.why: A CPD record shows what you have done and learned, demonstrates your development and informs the next round of planning.

whyNot.0: Recording captures reflection; it doesn't replace it.
whyNot.1: The record's main purpose is development, not disputes.
whyNot.2: Feedback is still a key way to find gaps.
